note: THE locked style for every video the production engine makes. How a video looks and sounds lives here and nowhere else. Per-video choices (which visual, which graphic, which words, which clip becomes a short) do NOT live here — they live in the agent-written plan.

doctrine.rule: Everything on screen must earn its place. If you cannot say why it is there in one plain sentence, it does not go on screen.
doctrine.canvas: Burnt orange backdrop. Everything sits on it; the orange shows around the edges.
doctrine.keepOut: Visuals never enter the caption band.
doctrine.screenRule: If they need to look at it, it takes the screen (frame 'full' or 'center'). If it only supports what you are saying, it shares the screen (frame 'left' or 'right').

icons.rule: Icons are not optional decoration — they are what makes a frame feel designed. Every data figure, list item, process step, node and label should carry a relevant icon.
icons.choose: Pick the icon by meaning, from the full Tabler set (menu.icons). Give each element its own icon; do not repeat the same icon across a row unless the meaning is identical.
icons.color: Icons inherit the brand colour: white on the canvas, brand-blue or orange for emphasis, matching the figure they sit with.
icons.restraint: Relevant and on-brand only. A wrong or generic icon is worse than none — but 'none' should be the rare exception, not the default.
icons.how: Diagrams: set `icon` on nodes/steps/items. Composition: add an `icon` node (name + optional color) next to its figure or label.

segments.rule: The video is an ordered list of segments: FOOTAGE (you talking — the face, no visuals) or SNAPSHOT (a b-roll section on the orange backdrop, one completed composition). Footage and b-roll are separated: the face shows only in footage segments and a snapshot always sits on the backdrop. Every narration beat is covered by exactly one segment.
segments.everySlot: In a snapshot, every element is hidden until its beat speaks it — every slot must be introduced by a beat, so nothing shows before its narration.

hook.rule: The hook is always FOOTAGE — you, talking to camera. The opening belongs to your face, never to a b-roll snapshot or a card.

editorial.principle: Change the visual only when the new visual gives more information, clarity, emphasis or narrative value than staying on the face.
editorial.stayOnFace: Stay on the face when another visual does not materially improve the communication.
editorial.gate: For each narration beat, find a concrete thing to see (number, name, screen, place, result, product), a structure the ear cannot hold (process, relationship, architecture, sequence, comparison), a payoff (stat, quote, takeaway, CTA), or the real thing worth showing. If none is true, stay on the face.

carrier.what: real action or subject you filmed
number, claim, takeaway, quote, CTA, title

editorial.frame: A graphic's frame comes from its template — never override it. A visual takes 'full' when they must inspect or read it, 'left'/'right' when it only supports what is said.
editorial.why: One sentence naming the value from the gate. The video must be worse without it.
editorial.timing: Enter on the words that need it, leave when they end. Hold long enough to read. One overlay at a time, no re-trigger in a beat.
editorial.motion: Only for a hit: one emphasis word per caption, one zoom 1.12-1.15 on a payoff, at most one sfx cue per overlay. Under a takeover the template already animates. Default is still.
editorial.keepTest: Delete it in your head. If the explanation is still complete, it was optional — delete it. Keep only what the explanation breaks without.
editorial.hook: The first 6 seconds are always you, talking to camera; no takeover overlay before the first sentence lands.

layout.note: The shared placement vocabulary. `safe` is the area a visual may occupy (its bottom excludes the caption band). `sizes` is the max box for each size token as a fraction of the canvas; `at` anchors that box inside the safe area. Text uses only the width, as a maximum content width — the text wraps below it and is never stretched to fill.

text.note: Free text the model may place (labels, titles). A size token is the maximum content width; the text wraps below it. Roles fix type so free text stays on brand.

composition.note: The composition language's design tokens — a video type scale (ratios of canvas width), the zones a visual may occupy, and surface tones. Derived from brand/tokens.css and the brand colours above. A composition (beat -> scene graph) resolves its roles against these, so every frame stays on brand without hardcoding.

motion.note: How a snapshot's beats animate. A beat's action.op (introduce/reveal/move/resize/restyle/retext/replace/highlight/hold) resolves against these; numeric figures count up to their exact value over countUp seconds. The root `motion` block is the fallback.

shape.note: Small geometric accents in brand tones: a bar (filled block), a line (thin rule), a box (outline), or a circle (dot).

media.note: How a media element (image or video) is cropped inside its resolved frame. `fit` is contain (whole media, letterboxed) or cover (fill the frame, crop the overflow). `focus` picks the kept region of a cover crop (object-position). `camera` is the media's own deterministic pan/zoom across its on-screen window — the media moves inside its frame, unlike the element `motion` which animates the frame in. `overscan` is the extra scale a pan keeps so no empty edge is ever revealed.

backdrop.note: The designed backdrop, the base layer of every composition. A grid with depth. Edit the SVG to change the look; every future video follows. brand.colors.bg is the fallback if the file is missing.

output.note: Used by both the cleaner's cut and the render, so the final size is predictable. crf 18 is visually lossless; preset veryfast is the speed choice for this machine. The picture is encoded at most twice: once by the cleaner, once by the render.

audio.note: Loudness target applied to every render (preview and final) after the picture is encoded. loudnessI is the integrated target in LUFS; truePeak is the ceiling in dBTP. HyperFrames renders the voice low, so this brings it to a social-standard level. Set normalize:false to skip.

render.note: The engine owns how HyperFrames renders, so it never guesses. workers and fps are passed explicitly; this overrides HyperFrames' low-memory pin and its auto worker sizing. On an 8 GB machine, floor(RAM*0.5/1536MB) = 2 workers is the safe ceiling; more spills to the page file and slows the render. lowMemoryMode:false keeps hardware GPU capture (low-memory mode would force software). timeoutMs is the spawnSync budget. preview is the fast, low-res canvas the agent iterates on (no asset, no gate); final is the locked, full-res render. --experimental-fast-capture is NOT used: drawElement self-verification fails on this composition.

clean.note: How the cleaner turns raw footage into one cleaned video. Silences are measured from the audio, never guessed from the transcript, so a word the model missed is never cut. The cleaner shows the cut list and never cuts without a human yes. gapMin = shortest silence worth trimming (s). gapKeep = silence left after the previous word (s). minCut = shortest pause cut allowed (s). cutPadEnd = silence left before the next word (s). edgeKeep = silence left at the very start and end (s). pad = room left around a filler, self-talk or false-start cut (s). minKeep = a kept clip shorter than this is absorbed into a cut (s). utteranceGap = silence that ends a spoken line (s). fillers = words removed on sight. selfTalk = asides said to himself, matched on the words themselves, so a countdown stuck to the start of a line is removed on its own. selfTalkExact = single words removed only when the whole line is that one word. tags = phrases of a watermark baked into the audio (e.g. Auphonic's free tag), removed only at the very start or end; tag = gap that still counts as one tag and how close to the start/end it must be. retake = false starts: maxGap = how close (s) a short line and the line that repeats it must be, similarity = word overlap that marks two lines as the same, maxWords = words compared per line, shortStart = a line this short that the next repeats from the top. repeat = a line said more than once: keep the last try and remove the first try plus everything said up to the last try; window = how far apart (s) the tries can be, maxAhead = how many spoken lines ahead to look, minWords = lines shorter than this are never treated as repeats, minPrefix = same opening words that mark two lines as the same, shortLine = a line this short repeated from the top is the same line, orphanGap = a short fragment this close (s) before a try joins its cut. inline = a phrase said twice in one breath: maxWords = longest repeated phrase to look for, minWords = shortest (1 catches 'the the'), gapWords = words allowed between the copies.

center.what: big stat, quote, CTA, title, prompt

left.what: a supporting visual or note; face on the right

right.what: a supporting visual or button; face on the left

framesPortraitNote: On a tall (9:16) canvas every overlay fills the whole screen and covers the video. There is no side-by-side split on tall video: a supporting note, a card, a diagram, or b-roll all become full screen. The face is hidden while the overlay plays. This is the permanent rule for portrait; the four names are kept so plans and templates stay valid, but they resolve to the same full-screen slot.

full.what: screenshots, screen recordings, diagrams, charts (full screen)

center.what: big stat, quote, CTA, title, prompt (full screen)

left.what: a supporting visual or note (full screen on tall video)

right.what: a supporting visual or button (full screen on tall video)

footage.note: Footage is a first-class visual segment (the face), the same rank as a snapshot. The engine derives it from the narration: a snapshot is on screen only while its content is building and shown (its first body element to its last), and every remaining stretch — a lead-in, a gap between snapshots, the hook, the tail — becomes footage, snapped to the exact narration words. A gap shorter than minGapSeconds is not worth a cut: the previous scene holds across it so b-roll stays seamless — keep this high enough that the face never flashes for a second or two between two b-rolls. A snapshot on screen shorter than minSnapshotSeconds is extended (the composition holds longer) so a b-roll never flickers.

motion.note: A gap shorter than takeoverHoldGapSeconds between two take-over scenes is not real face time: the face stays hidden across the whole run, so back-to-back b-roll reads as one visual block instead of flashing the footage at the seam. A gap of this length or longer returns the face; a split or a speaker:keep inside the gap always returns it.

voice.rule: Talk to the human in plain, short sentences. No technical words. No status reports full of terms. Say what happened and what you need, in as few words as possible.
never: the plan failed validation on 2 constraints
instead: Ready. Should I do the shorts?
One thing is off — the second card runs too long. Fix it?
Done. Two shorts cut. Want to see them?
